video_title: Asia Stocks Fall From Record as Tech Rally Cools | The China Show 6/23/2026
gist: A violent de-risking session in Asian memory names (Kospi -4%+, sidecar triggered) is diagnosed less as a fundamental break than as a market-structure problem, with guests detailing $22bn of leveraged single-stock ETFs on S.K. Hynix and a >200% tracking gap in Hong Kong's now-largest ETP. Alongside, Hao Hong of Lotus Asset Management calls the growth-vs-value extreme a 2021 analog and forecasts rotation into Chinese value within two months, while the show works through Iran's 60-day oil-sale license, a hawkish new Fed chair, Hong Kong's $22bn IPO year, and battery/biofuel supply-chain disruption from Summer Davos.

themes.theme: Korea memory unwind and single-stock leverage

insights.claim: The Kospi fell 4.2% with S.K. Hynix and Samsung Electronics leading the drag ahead of Micron earnings, and the Korea Exchange activated its sidecar mechanism to halt Kosdaq program selling for five minutes.
insights.speaker: Avril Hong / Haidi Stroud-Watts (hosts)
insights.so_what: A circuit-breaker-level move in the region's most crowded AI proxy is the cleanest real-time read on how fragile memory positioning has become into quarter-end.

insights.claim: Asian-time-zone chip trading is far more leveraged and retail-heavy than the US session, which is why Samsung fell 3% intraday and Korean names swung in a 50% high-to-low range despite Micron's strength in New York.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens (Bloomberg markets reporter)
insights.so_what: Positioning, not fundamentals, explains the Asia-US gap in chip tape — fade Asian-hours capitulation unless US pricing confirms it.
insights.quote: THE TRADERS IN THE ASIAN TIME ZONE ARE MUCH MORE LEVERAGED AND MUCH MORE RETAIL HEAVY.

insights.claim: Micron has led the market by a wide margin into an earnings print with very high expectations, making pre-event profit-taking the logical risk-management trade across the Asian memory complex.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens (Bloomberg markets reporter)
insights.so_what: Micron's print is the single binary event that resets the whole Asia memory trade; size risk accordingly rather than chasing the dip beforehand.

insights.claim: There are 40 leveraged ETFs on S.K. Hynix alone holding over $22 billion in assets, much of it gathered in just the last couple of weeks, and these products amplify volatility while occupying a disproportionate share of trading volume.
insights.speaker: David (Bloomberg strategist, Hong Kong)
insights.so_what: Mechanical daily rebalancing on this asset base means down days get exaggerated — a structural reason to expect fatter tails in Korean chip names than fundamentals justify.
insights.quote: IF WE LOOK AT THE LARGEST STOCK IN SOUTH KOREA, S.K. HYNIX, 40 LEVERAGED E.T.F.’S ON JUST THAT STOCK ALONE HAVE ASSETS OVER $22 BILLION.

insights.claim: The S.K. Hynix 2x leveraged ETP has surpassed the Tracker Fund to become Hong Kong's largest ETP by assets and the third-largest leveraged ETP globally, after returning almost 900% year-to-date.
insights.speaker: Rebecca (senior analyst, Bloomberg Intelligence)
insights.so_what: A single-stock leveraged product becoming a market's largest fund is itself a late-cycle sentiment marker worth tracking as a crowding gauge.
insights.quote: IT’S RETURNED ALMOST 900% YEAR-TO-DATE BUT ALSO ONE OF THE LARGEST PRODUCTS ACROSS THE GLOBE NOW.

insights.claim: The S.K. Hynix 2x ETP has run a more than 200% year-to-date tracking difference versus its theoretical value because daily resets plus swap costs — banks are struggling to find protection as the fund ballooned — get embedded back into the fund, with investors paying over 1% on some days just for access.
insights.speaker: Rebecca (senior analyst, Bloomberg Intelligence)
insights.so_what: Total cost of ownership, not headline performance, is the real return driver here — the compounding drag argues against holding these products as anything but short-dated trades.
insights.quote: WE CALCULATED THAT YEAR-TO-DATE THERE’S MORE THAN A 200% TRACKING DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE THEORETICAL VALUE OF WHERE THE FUND SHOULD BE, VERSUS THE UNDERLYING S.K. HYNIX.

insights.claim: After more than eight Korean issuers launched the same single-stock leveraged ETF and prices dislocated to premiums and discounts as high as 40-50%, Korea's regulator has publicly expressed regret at not blocking them, making new rules such as creation halts or size limits a live possibility.
insights.speaker: Rebecca (senior analyst, Bloomberg Intelligence)
insights.so_what: Regulatory intervention in these products is a distinct, non-fundamental risk to Korean chip flows — and a potential forced-unwind catalyst.

themes.theme: China's K-shaped market: AI hardware versus consumer

insights.claim: China's AI buildout is a much more capital-light version built on open-source software, so the capex numbers going into China look more sustainable and steady than the US equivalent.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens (Bloomberg markets reporter)
insights.so_what: Argues Chinese AI names carry less capex-obsolescence risk than US hyperscalers, supporting relative allocation to China AI over US AI infrastructure.

insights.claim: In both Chinese markets the 52-week low list is full of consumer names while the 52-week high list is full of semiconductor supply-chain names, a dispersion Bloomberg's markets reporter expects to keep widening.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens (Bloomberg markets reporter)
insights.so_what: Index-level China exposure masks the real trade; long semis versus short consumer has been the working expression and is being flagged to persist.
insights.quote: THE 52-WEEK LOW LIST IN BOTH MARKETS IS FULL OF CONSUMER NAMES. THE 52 WEEK RECORD HIGH LIST IN BOTH MARKETS IS FULL OF SEMI CONDUCTOR SUPPLY CHAIN NAMES.

insights.claim: SMIC is a fraction of the size of Micron and Intel, so US semiconductor market caps are the reference point for how far the Chinese semiconductor trade can still run.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens (Bloomberg markets reporter)
insights.so_what: A relative-market-cap frame gives a concrete upside anchor for Chinese semi names rather than a vague momentum call.
insights.quote: NAMES LIKE SMIC ARE A FRACTION OF THE SIZE OF MICRON AND INTEL

insights.claim: The key swing factor for Chinese equity leadership is whether Beijing chooses to stimulate the semiconductor ecosystem or pivot to a consumer-adoption strategy, which would trigger sector rotation.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens (Bloomberg markets reporter)
insights.so_what: Policy direction, not earnings, is the rotation trigger to watch — read stimulus announcements as sector-allocation signals.

insights.claim: Chinese tech hardware and semiconductor-related export growth is running up 40-50% year on year with export prices surging as well, even as the overall Chinese market index has lagged US peers this year.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: Rising volumes and rising prices together signal genuine pricing power in Chinese tech hardware exports — a fundamental underpin rather than pure multiple expansion.
insights.quote: EXPORT GROWTH IS UP YEAR ON YEAR 40%, 50% AND EXPORT PRICES ARE SURGING AS WELL.

insights.claim: The relative outperformance of Chinese growth, tech hardware and semiconductor names over traditional value names has reached an extreme seen only once before in history, in early 2021.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: The 2021 analog is a warning that the current leadership is stretched; use it to time reduction in crowded China growth exposure.
insights.quote: OUTPERFORMANCE HAS REACHED A VERY SORT OF EXTREME THAT WE HAVE NOT SEEN IN THE PAST HISTORY. ONLY ONCE, THAT WAS AN EARLY 2021.

insights.claim: Hao Hong expects a sector rotation out of Chinese growth and into traditional value sectors within roughly the next two months, with money then hunting the low valuations available especially in Hong Kong.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable rotation call: position for Hong Kong value re-rating as Korea/Taiwan semi extremes mean-revert.
insights.quote: WE ARE EXPECTING A SECTOR ROTATION TOWARDS THE TRADITIONAL VALUE SECTOR PROBABLY IN THE NEXT TWO MONTHS OR SO.

insights.claim: Since early 2023 newly created money on the PBOC balance sheet has been flowing into semiconductors and high-growth sectors rather than the traditional economy, with fixed-asset and real estate investment falling at double-digit year-on-year rates — an outcome Hao Hong frames as good news rather than a problem.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: Reframes weak Chinese property data as a deliberate credit-reallocation rather than a policy failure — bad macro headlines need not mean bad equity outcomes in the favoured sectors.

insights.claim: The removal of subsidies for electronics and cars cut Chinese retail sales growth by 1.5 percentage points via EV sales, leaving retail sales flat year on year, while service spending rose nearly 6% and beat expectations — meaning much real consumption is simply not captured in the retail sales figure.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: The consensus 'Chinese consumer is dead' read is a measurement artifact; experience-led consumption plays (travel, concerts, camping) may be mispriced against the headline.
insights.quote: SO I THINK THE EV SALES THIS YEAR HAVE DRAGGED DOWN THE RETAIL SALES GROWTH BY 1.5 PERCENTAGE POINTS.

insights.claim: The Hang Seng index of companies with revenue outside mainland China is outperforming the MSCI China index, showing that offshore revenue exposure — not domestic demand — is the winning factor in Chinese equities.
insights.speaker: Haidi Stroud-Watts (host)
insights.so_what: A screenable factor: overweight Chinese listings with overseas revenue while the domestic consumer and real estate remain flagging.

insights.claim: JD.com's chief economist frames China as running three simultaneous divergences — strong external demand (exports around 10%, reserves close to $3.5 trillion) against soft internal demand, new industries like high tech and new energy against declining old industries like real estate, and investment against consumption.
insights.speaker: JD.com chief economist
insights.so_what: A three-axis map for allocating within China that explains why aggregate GDP-style calls keep missing the equity outcome.

insights.claim: China's currency is still around 10-20% undervalued and Christine Lagarde has said China needs to look at it, but Beijing is stubborn about the pace of appreciation and FX volatility is very low because nobody expects China to do what trading partners demand.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens (Bloomberg markets reporter)
insights.so_what: Cheap FX vol plus a structurally undervalued currency makes long-dated CNY appreciation optionality attractive; European luxury and autos are the levered losers while it stays weak.
insights.quote: EUROPE NEED SOME HELP EXPORTING TO CHINA AND CHINA'S FX IS STILL READY TO BE AROUND 10%, 20% UNDERVALUED STILL.

insights.claim: With the Chinese currency trading well below the critical 6.8 level, Hao Hong is looking for appreciation to at least 6.5 and beyond, driven by trade terms and record-breaking exports.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: An explicit FX target that, if hit, mechanically boosts USD returns on Chinese assets and supports the Hong Kong re-rating thesis.
insights.quote: WE ARE LOOKING FOR THE YEN TO CONTINUE TO APPRECIATE TO AT LEAST 6.5 AND BEYOND.

insights.claim: China is generating roughly $1.2 trillion of trade surplus yet reserve growth is lagging well behind it, which Hao Hong reads as a large stock of Chinese money sitting offshore hunting returns — with capital account and direct-investment data now showing it starting to come back.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: The surplus-reserves gap is a quantifiable pool of repatriable capital — its return is the flow mechanism behind both a stronger currency and a Chinese equity re-rating.

insights.claim: Chinese regulators' severe crackdown on illegal cross-border trading forces offshore money back into the domestic market, which Hao Hong says bodes well for both the currency and Chinese equity revaluation.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: A regulatory crackdown usually read as a negative is here a forced-buying catalyst for onshore assets.

insights.claim: China still controls about 80% of global rare earth production, giving it a strong bargaining chip in US negotiations and already cutting exports to Japan, while US alternatives such as Greenland mines will take years to permit and ramp.
insights.speaker: Hao Hong (managing partner, Lotus Asset Management)
insights.so_what: Rare earth names retain a multi-year competitive moat; the leverage also caps how far US export controls can escalate.
insights.quote: RIGHT NOW CHINA STILL CONTROLS ABOUT 80% OF THE GLOBAL RARE EARTH PRODUCTION AND IS IN A VERY STRONG POSITION TO NEGOTIATE.

themes.theme: Iran oil license and the Hormuz reopening

insights.claim: Washington has issued a 60-day license allowing Iran to sell oil on the international market to essentially anyone including the US, the first major action to emerge from the memorandum of understanding signed last week.
insights.speaker: Laura Davison (Bloomberg, Washington)
insights.so_what: A two-month supply window with a hard expiry — the license lapse date is a defined catalyst for a crude repricing.

insights.claim: There are visible cracks between US and Iranian messaging — the US says nuclear inspectors will be allowed in and that Iran will use frozen assets to buy US agricultural commodities, while Iran calls the first false and has not confirmed the second.
insights.speaker: Laura Davison (Bloomberg, Washington)
insights.so_what: Contradictory readouts mean the ceasefire premium in oil and risk assets is more fragile than the headline deal implies.

insights.claim: With the war unpopular and Republicans defending House and Senate majorities in November, criticism that the Iran deal is too generous creates political pressure on the administration to keep gas prices falling and show wins.
insights.speaker: Laura Davison (Bloomberg, Washington)
insights.so_what: Midterm politics biases US policy toward lower energy prices into November — a headwind for sustained crude upside.

insights.claim: The US president says more oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz yesterday than ever before and the strait is totally open while negotiations continue.
insights.speaker: clip, U.S. president
insights.so_what: Record throughput removes the supply-shock bid from crude and shifts the price driver back to demand, which China consumption data now dominates.
insights.quote: WE HAVE AN OPEN STRAIT AND WE HAVE A COUNTRY THAT WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON

themes.theme: Hawkish Fed, flattening curve and Asian rate pressure

insights.claim: The Fed came out last week considerably more hawkish than the market expected, particularly the new Fed chairman, and is reacting to the level of inflation today rather than the forward path — with this week's PCE likely to reinforce that inflation is too high.
insights.speaker: David (Bloomberg strategist, Hong Kong)
insights.so_what: A backward-looking reaction function means near-term data keeps the hawkish tilt intact regardless of the improving oil-driven outlook.

insights.claim: With the US short end selling off on the hawkish Fed while long-end yields have barely moved, the curve is flattening — and if that persists, duration looks more attractive for anyone worried about equity volatility as oil trends lower.
insights.speaker: David (Bloomberg strategist, Hong Kong)
insights.so_what: An explicit trade: own long-end duration as an equity-vol hedge while headline inflation rolls over with crude.
insights.quote: IF THAT CONTINUES TO PERSIST, I THINK DURATION PERHAPS LOOKS MORE ATTRACTIVE

insights.claim: Renewed dollar strength is pushing up import prices and inflation across Asia, pressuring Asian central banks to turn hawkish, but South Korea's leveraged market structure limits how far its central bank can push rates without threatening financial conditions.
insights.speaker: David (Bloomberg strategist, Hong Kong)
insights.so_what: Korea is caught between imported inflation and domestic leverage — an argument for policy paralysis and continued currency weakness rather than decisive hikes.

insights.claim: Korea, like Japan, faces upside rate risk as its government has to start dealing with inflation driven by the AI boom itself.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens (Bloomberg markets reporter)
insights.so_what: The AI capex cycle is becoming a macro rate risk in its host economies — a second-order drag on the same equity markets it has lifted.

insights.claim: Dollar-yen is pinned near 162, its weakest level in about four decades, with the Japanese finance minister confirming a call with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and one trader saying the hurdle for intervention is not high.
insights.speaker: Bloomberg hosts
insights.so_what: Intervention risk is asymmetric and near-term at these levels; short-yen carry positions carry gap risk into any coordinated action.

insights.claim: Christine Lagarde says the Iran war shock is too large for the ECB to look through without jeopardizing its target, but sees no evidence yet of de-anchored inflation expectations or second-round effects that would warrant a more forceful policy response.
insights.speaker: Christine Lagarde (ECB, clip)
insights.so_what: The ECB is explicitly on hold-and-watch — euro rates should stay range-bound absent a wage or expectations break.
insights.quote: THE SHOCK IS TOO LARGE TO LOOK THROUGH WITHOUT JEOPARDIZING OUR TARGET. BUT WE SEE NO EVIDENCE YET OF THE ANCHORING OF INFLATION EXPECTATIONS

themes.theme: Hong Kong listings machine and Connect expansion

insights.claim: Hong Kong Exchange has taken about $22 billion of IPO proceeds and close to $38 billion of follow-on capital year to date heading into the last week of June, with Bloomberg Intelligence seeing it on track for a six-year high in 2026 listing proceeds.
insights.speaker: Johnson Choi (HKEX, head of global issuer services)
insights.so_what: Sustained primary issuance at this run-rate underwrites HKEX's own earnings and signals reopened risk appetite for Asian equity supply.
insights.quote: YEAR TO DATE WE’VE HAD ABOUT $22 BILLION OF I.P.O. PROCEEDS AND CLOSE TO ABOUT $38 BILLION FOLLOW-ON CAPITAL

insights.claim: Over 50% of Hong Kong's issuance this year has come from tech, broadening and deepening from AI infrastructure to platform to applications, with additional strong issuance from healthcare, industrials, new energy metals and mining, and consumer retail.
insights.speaker: Johnson Choi (HKEX, head of global issuer services)
insights.so_what: The listing mix is a forward window on which Asian sectors can access capital — and where secondary supply will land.

insights.claim: Hong Kong took seven international issuers last year from Southeast Asia, Africa, the US and Central Asia and now has over 10 international companies publicly filed, including an Indonesian gold company listing June 26 via a Hong Kong Depositary Receipt structure unused for about 12 years.
insights.speaker: Johnson Choi (HKEX, head of global issuer services)
insights.so_what: Reviving HDRs and courting non-China issuers is HKEX's hedge against mainland pipeline dependence — watch the June 26 deal as the template.

insights.claim: Southbound flows now account for effectively 20% of HKEX's daily turnover and continue strongly in both directions despite the mainland crackdown on illicit cross-border facilitators, because Stock Connect is the legal channel mainland authorities have reiterated.
insights.speaker: Johnson Choi (HKEX, head of global issuer services)
insights.so_what: The crackdown redirects rather than destroys flow, channelling it through Connect — structurally positive for HKEX volumes.
insights.quote: OUR SOUTHBOUND FLOWS IN TERMS OF OUR DAILY TURNOVER, OUR A.D.T. IS EFFECTIVELY 20% OF OUR DAILY VOLUME.

insights.claim: Hong Kong's financial secretary has told local state media that regulators are weighing expanded southbound Connect quotas and a long-discussed IPO Connect letting mainland retail investors buy Hong Kong IPOs directly, while HKEX has consulted the market on broadening confidential pre-revenue listings beyond biotech under its Chapter 18 specialist technology channel covering robotics, AI, hardware, green tech and potentially aerospace.
insights.speaker: Stephen Engle (Bloomberg) and Johnson Choi (HKEX)
insights.so_what: Both changes would materially expand Hong Kong's demand pool and issuer base — leading indicators for HKEX volumes and for where Asian aerospace and robotics capital gets raised.

themes.theme: Battery chemistry and biofuel supply-chain disruption

insights.claim: Pure Lithium's lithium metal battery replaces the graphite anode that makes up half the weight and volume of today's lithium-ion cells, delivering roughly double the energy density of batteries in current use.
insights.speaker: chairman and CEO, Pure Lithium
insights.so_what: If commercialized, it structurally impairs graphite demand and the anode supply chain built around it.

insights.claim: Because Pure Lithium's cell is manufactured in the charged state, it cuts capex by 40% and can be made in one day, versus over 500 days to get a lithium molecule out of the ground and into a conventional lithium-ion battery.
insights.speaker: chairman and CEO, Pure Lithium
insights.so_what: A one-day production cycle attacks the working-capital and lead-time moat of incumbent cell makers — the real competitive threat is speed, not just density.

insights.claim: Pure Lithium says a new electrolyte blended from available materials has achieved over 8,500 cycles, which would cut the levelized cost of energy storage by 75%.
insights.speaker: chairman and CEO, Pure Lithium
insights.so_what: A 75% LCOE cut would reset storage economics and the return profile of grid and microgrid projects — verify the cycle claim before underwriting it.
insights.quote: WE HAVE GOTTEN OVER 8500 CYCLES. THAT MEANS THE LEVELIZED COST OF ENERGY STORES CAN BE REDUCED BY 75%.

insights.claim: Against consensus enthusiasm, Pure Lithium's CEO argues solid-state batteries will not arrive in our lifetime because cells need some liquid to shuttle lithium ions, they are incredibly difficult and expensive to manufacture, and there is no evidence they are safer than a lithium metal cell with a little liquid.
insights.speaker: chairman and CEO, Pure Lithium
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the solid-state narrative embedded in many EV and battery valuations — worth stress-testing any position premised on solid-state timelines.
insights.quote: I DO NOT BELIEVE IT WILL HAPPEN IN OUR LIFETIME.

insights.claim: Sodium-ion has substantially less energy density because sodium is a bulky molecule, making it best suited to stationary or grid storage rather than vehicles.
insights.speaker: chairman and CEO, Pure Lithium
insights.so_what: Segments the next-gen battery race by end market — sodium-ion competes with storage economics, not with EV range.

insights.claim: Pure Lithium's battery avoids graphite, which is 95% produced in China, and uses no nickel or cobalt, while its next-generation cell uses palladium of which China is one of the largest producers — so the pitch is localized supply chains using ubiquitous materials rather than decoupling from China.
insights.speaker: chairman and CEO, Pure Lithium
insights.so_what: Reframes battery reshoring as a materials-substitution problem, and flags palladium as a potential new demand vector if the next-gen cell scales.
insights.quote: OUR BATTERY DOES NOT REQUIRE GRAPHITE WHICH IS 95% PRODUCED IN CHINA

insights.claim: Biofuels are already 4% of total world fuel consumption and cost-competitive — bioethanol against gasoline and biodiesel against diesel — with the Hormuz crisis acting only as a catalyzer of an existing shift as Brazil, Indonesia and China double up on decoupling from fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: CEO, biosolutions company (Summer Davos guest)
insights.so_what: Argues the biofuel bid survives normalization in oil prices, so don't fade biofuel exposure on a Middle East de-escalation.
insights.quote: THE CRISIS IN HORMUZ HAS ONLY BEEN A CATALIZER OF A CHANGE THAT’S ALREADY HAPPENING

insights.claim: Oracle reduced its global workforce over the last 12 months by more than previously known, incurring about $0.8 billion in restructuring costs, and stated in a filing that AI adoption and deployment may continue to lead to job losses.
insights.speaker: Bloomberg hosts (corporate news)
insights.so_what: A large-cap software firm explicitly attributing headcount reduction to AI is a template other enterprise software issuers are likely to follow — watch margin guidance, not revenue, for the AI effect.

insights.claim: Qualcomm is in advanced talks to acquire chip startup Modular for about $4 billion, a company that raised a $250 million round in September 2025, with a deal potentially reached in coming weeks though no final agreement exists.
insights.speaker: Bloomberg hosts (corporate news)
insights.so_what: A live datapoint on the private-to-public valuation markup in AI chip software and on Qualcomm's willingness to buy its way into the stack.

insights.claim: A large non-traded credit fund with roughly $21 billion in assets capped withdrawals for the second consecutive quarter after investors sought to redeem heavily, amid concerns about its exposure to software firms and AI.
insights.speaker: Bloomberg hosts (corporate news)
insights.so_what: Repeat gating in semi-liquid private credit is the clearest early sign that AI-adjacent credit exposure is being marked down where it cannot be sold.

insights.claim: SpaceX's three-day $600 billion rout led Wall Street losses and dragged Asian tech, while in Hong Kong an AI name fell 8.8% and MiniMax Group dropped close to 7% amid concerns about future revenue models as comparisons with Anthropic falter.
insights.speaker: Haidi Stroud-Watts (host)
insights.so_what: The de-rating is spreading from private AI marks into listed Asian AI model developers — revenue-model scrutiny, not compute demand, is the transmission channel.

insights.claim: Keir Starmer has resigned as Labour leader with Andy Burnham on course to become UK prime minister in the second half of July, and gilts and the pound rose on the resignation, leaving the choice of chancellor as the key market signal given very little budget wiggle room.
insights.speaker: Rosalind Mathieson (Bloomberg correspondent)
insights.so_what: The chancellor appointment is the tradable event for gilts and sterling — a left-flank pick reads as fiscal loosening, a centrist pick as continuity.
